To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the fluorescence of urine from patients with ovarian cancer is different compared to that of healthy individuals.

urine of patients with ovarian cancer has significantly reduced fluorescence intensity in the region of 330 nm excitation and 420 nm emission, and significantly increased fluorescence intensity in the regions of 370 nm excitation and either 440 or 420 nm emission.
the ratio of intensites of peaks at 370 nm excitation and 440 nm emission and at 330 nm excitation and at 420 nm emission is 18-times higher in urine of ovarian patients than in healthy urine.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the search for new markers of ovarian cancer.
the search for new markers for the early diagnosis of cancer.
development of a novel non-invasive method for ovarian cancer screening using the fluorescence excitemission matrices of urine.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fluorescence of urine is a potential tool for ovarian cancer diagnostics.
the fluorescence characteristics of urine excreted from ovarian cancer patients differ from those of healthy volunteers.
fluorescence spectroscopy of human urine is a promising tool for early diagnostics of ovarian cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fluorescence excitationemission matrices of undiluted urine from healthy volunteers are significantly different from those of ovarian cancer patients.
the fluorescence of human urine can serve as a non-invasive and non-destructive method for early diagnostics of ovarian cancer.
fluorescence spectroscopy of urine could be a valuable tool for the early detection of ovarian cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
fluorescence excitation-emissions matrices can be used for the early detection of ovarian cancer.
the fluorescence of urine can be used as an early diagnostic biomarker for ovarian cancer.
the fluorescence excitation–emission matrices (EEM) of undiluted urine of ovarian cancer patient differ from those of healthy volunteers.
